q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy in the form of heat and work.
e: True. Mechanical kinetic energy alone is not the whole subject. Thermodynamics studies systems whose energy appears as heat and work. A piston confining gas in a cylinder is the usual picture.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy exclusively in the form of mechanical kinetic energy.
e: False. Thermodynamics studies heat and work, not mechanical kinetic energy alone. A piston-and-gas cylinder is the usual example. Internal energy includes microscopic motion, not just bulk KE.

q: Thermal equilibrium is an important concept in thermodynamics.
e: True. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Zeroth law then lets a thermometer define that shared temperature.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is no net heat transfer between them.
e: True. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Two systems are in thermal equilibrium there cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is maximum net heat transfer between them.
e: False. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer. The two systems already share a temperature. Maximum flow would require a temperature difference.

q: Systems at the same temperature will be in thermal equilibrium with each other.
e: True. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Zeroth law then lets a thermometer define that shared temperature. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap.

q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that when two objects are separately in thermodynamic equilibrium with a third object, they all are in thermodynamic equilibrium with each other.
e: True. Zeroth law: if two objects are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. That is how temperature becomes a comparable property. A fourth object is not part of the statement.

q: The first law of thermodynamics is an application of the conservation energy for heat and thermodynamic processes.
e: True. Momentum or mass conservation is a different book. First law is conservation of energy applied to heat and thermodynamic processes. Delta U = Q - W, with W the work done by the system.

q: The first law of thermodynamics relates the change in internal energy of a system to heat added and the work done by the system.
e: True. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system minus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: True. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Change in internal energy Delta U of cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system plus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: False. First law is Delta U = Q minus W, not Q plus W, when W is work done by the system. You subtract the energy the system spends as work. Adding W would count that energy twice.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $Q$ is positive if heat is added to the system, and negative if heat is removed.
e: True. The two branches complement each other; they are not unrelated. Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $W$ is positive if work is done on the system, and negative if work is done by the system.
e: False. In this sign convention W is positive when the system does work, and negative when work is done on the system. Q is positive when heat is added. Flip those work signs and Delta U = Q - W fails.

q: The internal energy $U$ of a system is defined as the sum of the energies of all the constituent particles.
e: True. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U is the sum of the energies of all constituent particles. For an ideal gas that total tracks absolute temperature only.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure.
e: True. U is proportional to absolute temperature. An isothermal ideal-gas process therefore has Delta U = 0. Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on volume and pressure, not on temperature.
e: False. An ideal gas stores internal energy by temperature alone, not by volume or pressure. U is proportional to absolute temperature. Change V or p at fixed T and U stays put.

q: Internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
e: True. The monoatomic formula is U = (3/2) n R T. Inverse or exponential would not match that kinetic-theory count. Ideal-gas internal energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

q: Heat transfer and work are both energy in transit.
e: True. Heat and work are both energy in transit. Neither is stored as such inside the system. What stays behind is a change in internal energy.

q: Heat transfer and work are both stored as such in a system.
e: False. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored inventories. What the system stores is internal energy. After the process, you cannot point to a pile of heat or a pile of work inside.

q: Internal energy is a form of energy completely different from either heat or work.
e: True. Heat and work are path-dependent transfers. After the process you can quote U; you cannot quote a leftover pile of heat. Internal energy is a stored state property, different from heat or work.

q: A thermodynamic process may be defined as a change from one equilibrium state of a system to another.
e: True. Quasi-static means you crawl slowly enough to stay in internal equilibrium. A sudden bang is not that ideal path. A thermodynamic process is a change from one equilibrium state to another.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens slowly enough for the system to remain in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: True. You can then draw it as a curve on a p-V diagram and retrace it. Rapid processes jump off that curve. A quasi-static, or quasi-equilibrium, process is slow enough that the system remains in internal thermodynamic equilibrium.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens very rapidly to prevent the system from remaining in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: False. A quasi-static process is slow enough that the system stays in internal equilibrium. Rapid jumps throw it off the equilibrium path. Slow, not fast, is the reversible ideal.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.
e: True. Work done by the system is then p Delta V. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal. Isobaric means constant pressure.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant volume.
e: False. Isobaric means constant pressure. Constant volume is isochoric. At constant pressure the work is p Delta V.

q: The work done by the system in an isobaric process is simply the pressure multiplied by the change in volume.
e: True. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal. Isobaric means constant pressure. Work done by the system is then p Delta V.

q: An isochoric process occurs at constant volume.
e: True. For an ideal gas that heat is n Cv Delta T. Isochoric means constant volume, so W = p Delta V = 0. First law then says Delta U equals the heat that entered or left.

q: When the volume of a thermodynamic system is constant, no work is done by the system because $W = p \Delta V = 0$.
e: True. In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention. Heat added is positive Q.

q: According to the first law, in an isochoric process, the change in internal energy must equal any heat flowing into or out of the system.
e: True. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead.

q: An isothermal process occurs at a constant temperature.
e: True. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium.

q: For an ideal gas, internal energy $U$ is only a function of the volume.
e: False. For an ideal gas, U is a function of temperature only, not of volume. An isothermal ideal-gas process therefore has Delta U = 0. Volume can change while U stays fixed.

q: Internal energy is constant; therefore, $\Delta U$ is equal to zero for an isothermal process.
e: True. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q.

q: Since $\Delta U = 0$, according to the first law, $W = Q$ for an isothermal process.
e: True. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Since Delta U 0 according to the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is no heat transfer into or out of the system, i.e., $Q = 0$.
e: True. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out, often by insulating the system. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. Gamma = Cp/Cv then appears in the reversible adiabatic relations.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is maximum heat transfer into or out of the system.
e: False. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out. First law then collapses to Delta U = -W. Insulation, not a heat flood, is the adiabatic setup.

q: The first law of thermodynamics $\Delta U = Q - W$ is thus reduced to $\Delta U = -W$ for an adiabatic process.
e: True. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out, often by insulating the system. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. First law of thermodynamics Delta U Q cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: An adiabatic process can be done by enclosing the system in a thermal insulator.
e: True. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. Gamma = Cp/Cv then appears in the reversible adiabatic relations. Low thermal conductivity means a poor conductor, a thermal insulator.
